quote: Research has shown that we automatically assign to good-looking individuals such favorable traits as talent, kindness, honesty, and intelligence
content: For honesty, Eagly et al. found little, and "honesty" should come off the list. The essay put the claim in its own words, and Fable is right that the essay's source did not support it. The rest of the catalogue holds up better than "greatest hits" suggests. Hamermesh and Biddle's beauty premium appeared in the American Economic Review and has been replicated across countries. Mazzella and Feingold's meta-analysis found that attractive defendants were less likely to be convicted and received more lenient sentences, small effects that point the way the essay says (Mazzella & Feingold 1994). Stewart's courtroom observations are a published field study. The effects are smaller than the anecdotes, which is what shrinkage looks like, and the essay's conclusion concerns their direction.

quote: And—I know you don’t think you have to do it, but maybe you should—be just a little more skeptical of the more attractive political candidates.
content: A competence judgment made in one second from a face is a halo effect: a trait inferred from appearance. Todorov's result extends the essay's mechanism rather than replacing it. The attractiveness channel in elections is also well measured. In Finnish elections with many candidates on the ballot, rated beauty was a stronger predictor of votes than rated competence or trustworthiness (Berggren, Jordahl & Poutvaara 2010). So both cues leak, and which one matters more depends on how much else voters know. The essay's general rule covers both: "You should be suspicious if the people you know seem to separate too cleanly into devils and angels." Its closing line names the cue it had evidence for. A reader who follows the general rule catches competence-looking faces too.
